title: Stock Exchange
tagline: How the securities market works, the functions of a stock exchange, and the role of SEBI in regulating it. Unit weight: 5 marks.

overview.intro: A stock exchange converts a claim on a company into something a saver can buy in small units and sell again in minutes. That liquidity is what allows ordinary households to fund enterprise instead of leaving it to banks and large institutions. This five-mark unit explains the stock exchange and its functions, the process by which securities are issued and traded, the mechanism of a stock exchange transaction, and the role of the Securities and Exchange Board of India in protecting investors, regulating the market and promoting it.

learningOutcomes: Define the stock exchange and state its functions.
Explain the primary and secondary market distinction.
Describe the mechanism of a stock exchange transaction.
Explain the protective, regulatory and developmental functions of SEBI.
State the need for regulation of the securities market.

learn.title: The stock exchange and its functions

blocks.text: A stock exchange is an organised market, regulated and recognised under law, in which securities are bought and sold according to stated rules. It is organised because trading happens at a fixed place under a constitution rather than between strangers; it is a market because price is discovered there by the meeting of buyers and sellers; and it is regulated because the price formed there affects investment decisions across the economy. Membership is restricted to recognised brokers, and only securities admitted to dealings by the exchange may be traded on it.

blocks.caption: Functions of a stock exchange
rows: Converts household savings into investment in enterprises
Lets an investor convert a holding into cash quickly at a known market price
Continuous auction fixes a fair price for each security
The level and direction of the index reflect business confidence
Deals are done under rules, with regulated brokers and settlement
A falling price penalises poor management publicly

items: The exchange gives ready marketability, which is what makes equity attractive to hold.
Pricing is continuous, so the value of an investment is known at any time.
By admitting only companies that meet its listing requirements, it screens disclosures.
The index serves as a reference for funds, insurers and policy makers.

learn.title: Primary market, secondary market and the mechanism

blocks.text: The primary market is where a company raises fresh capital by issuing shares or debentures to the public, and the money flows to the company. The secondary market is where those already issued securities change hands between investors, and the money flows from buyer to seller rather than to the company. Both are needed: the primary market cannot function without the assurance that the security can later be sold, which is exactly what the secondary market provides.

blocks.caption: Primary market against secondary market
rows: Issue through banks, brokers or an offer document
Fixed at issue or by book building
Determined continuously by demand and supply
To enter or exit a holding

blocks.text: The mechanism of a transaction on the exchange follows a set order. The investor places an order through a member broker, who routes it to the trading floor or electronic system where it is matched against the opposite order, and a price is struck. The contract note confirms the trade, the transaction is recorded in the depository account through the clearing corporation, and settlement delivers the securities and the money on the settlement date.

items.text: An investor buys 500 shares through a broker at a price struck on the exchange.
items.note: The seller receives the money and the buyer receives the shares; the company is not party to this transaction at all.

items.text: A company making a public issue of new shares.
items.note: This is the primary market, and the proceeds reach the company to fund its operations.

blocks.text: The Securities and Exchange Board of India was set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body and given statutory powers in 1992 to protect the interests of investors in securities, to regulate the securities market, and to promote the development of the market. Its functions are usually grouped in three ways. Protective functions include registering and regulating brokers and merchant bankers, prohibiting fraudulent and unfair trade practices, and undertaking investor education. Regulatory functions include framing rules, approving stock exchange bylaws, inspecting books, and calling for information. Developmental functions include promoting the stock exchange, encouraging electronic trading, and developing the secondary market.

blocks.caption: SEBI’s three groups of functions
rows: Registration and regulation of intermediaries, prohibition of insider trading and unfair practices, investor education and grievance redress
Framing rules and model bylaws, approving changes to exchange bylaws, inspection of books, calling for information and records
Promotion of stock exchanges, encouragement of electronic and screen-based trading, development of the secondary market and investor protection funds

blocks.text: The need for regulation follows from the market’s own structure: information is unevenly distributed, intermediaries handle other people’s money, and a few participants can move prices that thousands rely on. Without a regulator, manipulation, misrepresentation and delay in settlement would drive honest investors out and raise the cost of capital for every honest company.

Regulation exists because three risks are intrinsic to securities trading. The first is information asymmetry: a promoter knows far more about a company than a retail buyer, which invites both innocent error and deliberate deception. The second is conflict of interest, since the intermediary who advises also earns from the transaction. The third is systemic risk, where the failure of one large participant unsettles every other. Regulation addresses each through disclosure requirements, separation of duties and surveillance of positions, and through settlement guarantees and penalties.

items: Disclosure: prospectus, quarterly results and material events made public.
Intermediary conduct: registration, capital adequacy and audit.
Market surveillance: monitoring of unusual price and volume movements.
Settlement guarantee: clearing corporation stands between buyer and seller.
Penalties: disgorgement, fines and debarment for manipulation and insider trading.

keyPoints: A stock exchange is an organised, regulated market for securities admitted to dealings.
It provides liquidity, capital formation, pricing, a barometer function and safety of transactions.
The primary market issues new securities and the proceeds go to the company.
The secondary market trades existing securities and the proceeds go to the seller.
The secondary market’s liquidity is what makes the primary market attractive.
A transaction runs order, matching, contract note, depository recording and settlement.
SEBI was established in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992.
SEBI’s functions are protective, regulatory and developmental.
Regulation is needed because of information asymmetry, conflicts of interest and systemic risk.
Insider trading and price manipulation are punished because they destroy investor confidence.
examFocus: Five marks: definition, three functions with a line each, and one clear distinction between primary and secondary market.
SEBI questions expect the three groups of functions, so classify before you describe.
In mechanism questions, mention the contract note and settlement, which are easy marks often missed.

questions.prompt: The function of a stock exchange that converts household savings into investment in enterprise is:
questions.explanation: Channeling savings into productive investment is capital formation, which is the exchange’s deepest contribution to the economy.

questions.prompt: When a company makes a fresh public issue of shares, the transaction takes place in:
questions.explanation: A fresh issue creates new securities and the proceeds go to the company, which is the primary market.

questions.prompt: In a secondary market transaction, the money paid by the buyer goes to:
questions.explanation: The secondary market trades existing securities between investors, so the seller receives the money and the company is not involved.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a protective function of SEBI rather than a regulatory one?
options: Framing rules for the conduct of the market
Prohibiting fraudulent and unfair trade practices
Inspecting the books of a listed company
questions.answer: Prohibiting fraudulent and unfair trade practices
questions.explanation: Protective functions are directed at investors and fair dealing, while framing rules, approving bylaws and inspecting books are regulatory powers.

questions.prompt: The statutory body that regulates the securities market in India, given statutory powers in 1992, is known by the initials __________ .
questions.explanation: SEBI was created in 1988 as a non-statutory body and given enforceable powers in 1992 to protect investors and regulate the market.

questions.prompt: The document issued by a broker confirming the terms of a transaction executed on the exchange is called a contract __________ .
questions.explanation: The contract note is the broker’s written confirmation of the security, quantity, price and parties, and it is the basis of any later dispute.

questions.prompt: State four functions of a stock exchange.
questions.answer: Four functions are: capital formation, which channels household savings into investment in enterprise; liquidity, which lets an investor convert a holding into cash quickly at a known price; pricing of securities, where continuous meeting of buyers and sellers establishes a fair price; and acting as a barometer of the economy, since the level and direction of the index reflect business confidence. Safety of transactions under regulated rules is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each function needs a line explaining the mechanism, since a bare list earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the primary market and the secondary market.
questions.answer: The primary market is where a company raises fresh capital by issuing new securities, so the money flows to the company and the price is fixed at issue. The secondary market is where those already issued securities change hands between investors, so the money flows from the buyer to the selling investor and the price is determined continuously by demand and supply. The secondary market’s liquidity is what makes investors willing to buy in the primary market at all.
questions.explanation: Three points of contrast are expected, and the link between the two markets earns the remaining marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the protective, regulatory and developmental functions of SEBI.
questions.answer: Protective functions safeguard investors and fair dealing: SEBI registers and regulates brokers, merchant bankers and other intermediaries, prohibits fraudulent and unfair trade practices including insider trading, educates investors and provides for grievance redress. Regulatory functions give it authority over the market’s structure: it frames rules and model bylaws for the stock exchanges, approves changes to those bylaws, inspects the books of listed companies and intermediaries, and calls for information and records. Developmental functions extend the market itself: SEBI promotes the stock exchanges, encourages screen-based and electronic trading, develops the secondary market and supports investor protection arrangements. Together the three groups serve the statutory purpose of protecting investors while allowing the market to grow, because a market that grows without protection eventually loses the participants it depends on.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all three groups with named examples, since vague descriptions of protecting investors cover only one third of the question.

questions.prompt: A listed company’s shares jump 40% in two days on heavy volume, immediately before it announces a major contract. Three directors sold shares in the week before the announcement. Identify the issues and explain how the regulatory framework addresses them.
questions.answer: The pattern shows two distinct problems. The price rise before the announcement suggests that information leaked into the market, so ordinary buyers purchased at rising prices while some participants already knew why. The directors’ sales immediately before the announcement are the classic signature of insider trading, since they dealt on price-sensitive information that the public did not have. SEBI addresses the first through disclosure requirements, which oblige the company to inform the exchange of material events immediately rather than when convenient, and through market surveillance that flags unusual price and volume movements for investigation. It addresses the second by regulating intermediaries and listed companies, requiring promoters and directors to disclose their holdings and trades, and by charging and penalising insider trading with disgorgement of profits, fines and debarment. The exchange contributes through its listing agreement and by pausing trading where needed. The economic reason for all of this is that information asymmetry of this kind destroys confidence, and a market without confident participants cannot raise capital for anyone.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify both the leakage and the dealing, then map each to a specific regulatory instrument rather than asserting that SEBI regulates.
